# Withheld tribunal reasoning — [2026] UKFTT 351 (GRC)
# Gold-labelling material; NEVER include in a prompt.

# Manual cut: paragraphs 37-70 contain the tribunal's own analysis.
# The document had no section-level headings recognised by the fetch tool (all
# content was in a single (preamble) block). Analysis begins at para 37 with
# the tribunal's own interpretation of "Terms of Reference".

37. The parties have made submissions on the meaning of ToR. To summarise:- (a) the Appellant puts forward a dictionary definition that it is "the scope and limitations of an activity or area of knowledge." He adds (17):- "Thus, any documentation appertaining to the review that meets this definition would fall within the requirements of section 1 of the FOIA. However, it is possible that my use of the words pre-specified might have confused things. I chose those words because I wanted to make it clear that I was not seeking the final review report (which would be likely to contain the sort of information that would appear in terms of reference). However, in many reviews, there is an initial "scoping phase" of the review, after which terms of reference are formulated. It was certainly not my intention to seek only terms of reference that had been drawn up before commencement of the review." (b) DVLA in its response (42) says that there is no general legal definition but section 5(6) of the 2005 Act is helpful. DVLA says that ToR will "generally define the purpose of the review, the specific issues it will consider, who will be in charge of the review, the procedure to be adopted in carrying out the review and what the review's "end product" will be" . As for "pre- specified" DVLA refers again to the 2005 Act and say that it " implies the existence of a specific document, prepared before the review begins (usually following the commissioning of the review)." (c) the Appellant does not consider the 2005 Act to be helpful and prefers an approach which is to ask "how do you know one when you see one?" and he provides a list of the types of things one might find in a ToR. In effect he suggests that those with relevant experience will know one when they see one. (d) in his skeleton the Appellant said his own definition is "11...a written document providing guidance to those undertaking the work on what is expected them" and at the hearing Mr Chatham said that he agreed this definition. (e) in his statement Mr Chatham said that the Pro-Forma was not a ToR because "13...Instead, the Pro-Forma sets out the background to the proposal and its anticipated benefits and impacts." (f) at the hearing Mr Chatham said that the Draft Submission was not a ToR being at the scoping stage and a ToR might have been prepared if DVLA had been asked to go ahead with a project to remove the surrender requirement.

38. In our view ToR can mean different things to different people and in different contexts and all versions of the meaning presented to us and more could be right at times. We have been told of the 2005 Act meaning relevant to inquiries and we know the Appellant's meaning based on his experience. However some organisations might use different words prescribed by rules or tradition to say the same thing and such words might in some circumstances be in a contract or might be term of art in a particular field. We expect, if asked, a search-engine would suggest very many different definitions and all could be valid.

39. Also seeking to define, and thus limit, the meaning in these words risks taking an overly legalistic approach to a request. If in doubt DVLA could have sought clarity about the words used. However when asking for clarity on 12 January 2022 DVLA said "... Can you state what your case is in regards to and which copy of the terms of reference for that review is in regards to?" This may have given the impression that there was no doubt about what a ToR was and the need for clarity was about to "which copy.." the Request related. It is also possible that no doubts were raised about the meaning of the words because people tend to "know" what they think they mean in their particular context. It is probable that the risk of there being different possible interpretations was not identified and considered at the point the Request was made and the response was being prepared. This may also have been because at that stage DVLA reported that it held material in-scope. In-scope time frame

40. Whatever ToR means in this context it is important for there to be clarity about the time-frame in which any information would be in-scope of the Request. On an analysis of the correspondence between the Appellant and DVLA from 12 November 2021 to the Request on 12 January 2022 the Appellant was seeking the (pre-specified) terms of reference for the review which was referred to, in DVLA's response, as being already underway ( "we are reviewing") . Therefore only material that pre-dated the 12 November 2021 can be in-scope. Also by section 1(4) FOIA "information" is (emphasis added):- "the information in question held at the time when the request is received, except that account may be taken of any amendment or deletion made between that time and the time when the information is to be communicated under subsection (1)(b), being an amendment or deletion that would have been made regardless of the receipt of the request."

41. Therefore, even if DVLA drafted ToR for a review after it had started that review and if the clarifying words "pre-specified " are ignored, the in-scope cut off date for any information is whether it was held when the Request was received on 12 January 2022. Is the Draft Submission in the closed bundle in-scope?

42. Our conclusion is that it is not in-scope because it was not held at the date the Request was received.

43. Its date was a matter of dispute and confusion which was understandably raised by the Appellant as being undermining of DVLA's "not held" position generally. These issues can be seen from the chronology below (emphases added):- (a) on 22 January 2022 DVLA asked for clarity about " which copy of the terms of reference for that review is in regards to?" (b) on 24 January 2022 DVLA said it held in-scope information (83). (c) on 11 February 2022 DVLA repeated that response after an internal review (88). (d) on 4 November 2022 (141) Mr Chatham on behalf of DVLA said to the IC during its investigation that it did not hold "t he information specified by Dr Wise, as there are no pre-specified terms of reference for the policy review in question. However, the information that is held is a draft version of a submission to government Ministers outlining the policy and legal issues..." (e) in the DN on 21 November 2022 the IC expressed concern that DVLA was seeking to withhold information that was created in September 2022 and did not appear to be within the parameters of the Request. (f) in its Response to the Appeal, as late as in June 2023 (4) after the DN was issued, DVLA pleaded that at the date the Request was received (January 2022) the Draft Submission was " identified by the DVLA as being potentially within its scope..." (g) in a footnote to this part of the Response DVLA said (40):- "1 The Commissioner, in paragraph 23 of the decision notice, referred to a later version of this document produced in August 2022. An earlier version of the Draft Submission had already been produced by January 2022, when the request was submitted." (h) Mr Chatham, in his statement said that the Draft Submission was created "no earlier than 8 September 2022" and he knew this from a review of the metadata which he exhibited (155).

44. Mr Chatham sought to explain how the above had occurred. In his statement he said that when DVLA said that it had in-scope information in its original response that was an error caused, in his words, by a failure of the process between the FOIA team and the DVLA policy team and this error was regrettably not picked up on review because, he assumes, that the correct due diligence was not done at that time. Both, he said, were the wrong decision.

45. Mr Chatham first became involved after the complaint had been made to the IC. He said the reasons the IC was provided with the Draft Submission was because he (despite the date on it):- "was not aware of the date of the Draft Submission's creation and mistakenly believed that this was the information referred to as being held at the time of the DVLA's original response to the request."

46. He also said that he was "9...unaware of this history at the time the DVLA filed its response to the Appellant's appeal to the First Tier Tribunal"

47. At the hearing he also said:- (a) the Draft Submission was not in existence at the date the Request was made but he had not been aware of this when he asked the IC to consider this document because he had not reviewed the metadata at this time. (b) in the closed hearing (and a copy of this was provided to the Appellant showing it) that despite the supposed uncertainty in fact the Draft Submission was clearly headed "xx September 2022" (c) he accepted his statement at para 16 was wrong when it referred to " 8 September " as the metadata refers to a "submission template" document being edited for 1 minute on 28 September 2022 and the date "created" is stated as being is 28 September 2022. (d) it was likely he approved DVLA's response to the appeal in June 2023 which referred to an "earlier version" .

48. Mr Chatham expressed his view that the Draft Submission was not in any event a ToR because it was a "draft ministerial submission" which he considered to be nothing more than a scoping exercise to present to a Minister.

49. We concluded that the information held in the CB actually dated "xx September 2022" on the top of its first page and with metadata showing activity on 28 September 2022 does itself post-date the Request and is not in-scope of the Request. However, as set out below it does not automatically follow from this that there was not an earlier version of this document. We have not had to consider whether section 35 FOIA is engaged in respect of this document. Is the Pro-Forma in-scope?

50. We again considered whether this item which we saw at CB13 – CB15 was in-scope as regards its date and if so its content. Mr Chatham at the appeal said that this document initiated the review probably from information gathered and is best described as an impact assessment document and an "overview" .

51. The Appellant has not seen it. He did however point out that (52):- 1) The DVLA description of the pro-forma at para 15 refers to it as setting out "the background, impacts and work needed" so that it definitely includes some of the material commonly associated with terms of reference (see my opening remarks above on identification of terms of reference). 2) It was produced at the inception of the Surrender Requirements project. 3) It appears to have set the direction for the project over the period since June 2020. It, therefore, contains at least some of the key elements of terms of reference."

52. DVLA in its response to the appeal says (41) "15. During the course of preparing its response to this appeal, the DVLA identified a further document produced in June 2020, "Regulatory proposal pro-forma" DVLA went on to say that this "15...set out for senior DVLA officials the background, impacts and work needed to remove the Surrender Requirement."

53. Mr Chatham in his statement (152) says DVLA considered the Pro-Forma at the time of the internal review but:- "13...we took the view that the Pro-Forma did not fall within the terms of the request as it did not set out terms of reference for the review. Instead, the Pro-Forma sets out the background to the proposal and its anticipated benefits and impacts."

54. Mr Chatham at the hearing said that in his view it was not a ToR based on the Appellant's definition.

55. Leaving to one side whether that suggests an inconsistency about when it was identified it is accepted that it was produced in June 2020 and therefore existed at the date the Request was received.

56. The IC was shown the Pro-Form who, by reference to their understanding of the meaning of ToR, said that their view was that it was not a ToR but the Tribunal will wish to consider it and reach its own conclusion which may differ (CB16).

57. As it is possible for ToR to mean different things by different people and in different contexts it was reasonable for DVLA to reach their conclusion based on their use of these words. However we have read it with a broader definition in mind from which we concluded from it's content that it does have hallmarks of a ToR. In our view it does more than this but a document which sets out the background to a proposal and describes the work to be done its impact and anticipated benefits might reasonably be called by some (even if not DVLA) a ToR.

58. Therefore in our view it is a ToR for these purposes. It is therefore in-scope and should be disclosed in response to the Request. DVLA has not specifically made submissions on whether the Pro-Forma is, in their view, subject to an exemption and we do not know if they would wish to do so. An opportunity is therefore provided to do so in the substituted DN. On the balance of probabilities did DVLA hold any in-scope material at the date of the Request?

59. Despite DVLA's position being that they do not hold any in-scope material we were not, on the balance of probabilities, satisfied on this question because of the aggregation of the reasons that follow. The IC's view

60. Although ultimately satisfied that DVLA did not hold any in-scope information it is of note that in the DN the IC said (8) that it could not reasonably conclude that DVLA had conducted proper searches and therefore DVLA had failed to comply with section 1 FOIA. The Draft Submission in the CB

61. DVLA twice responded to the Request saying it held in-scope information and we were not able to hear from those who gave those responses with their explanation. DVLA were inaccurate when dealing with it and went through several changes of its position regarding it. Mr Chatham accepted his statement contained a typographical error about the metadata and that somehow the fact that the document had an actual date on it was overlooked. A draft submission

62. Of note is that, knowing that the IC at para 23 of the DN had pointed out the Draft Submission was dated long after the Request was received, DVLA in its response said:- "The Commissioner, in paragraph 23 of the decision notice, referred to a later version of this document produced in August 2022. An earlier version of the Draft Submission had already been produced by January 2022 , when the request was submitted."

63. Mr Chatham says that this error arose because he "was unaware of this history at the case the DVLA filed its response to the Appellant's appeal to the First Tier Tribunal". We could not see how, not knowing about the history, would itself enable DVLA to plead a positive case that there was an earlier version produced in January 2022. Additionally Mr Chatham accepted that the version in the CB would not have emerged from nothing and that something must have come before.

64. From what we were told by Mr Chatham in the closed hearing it is quite possible that there were earlier versions of the draft submission and it is quite possible that an earlier version existed in January 2022 as stated in DVLA's response. It maybe that any such earlier version(s) were deleted when new versions were created.

65. We were not satisfied that an appropriate search had been carried out to see if a version of the Draft Submission existed when the Request was received and we do not discount the possibility that it was. Process generally

66. Mr Chatham was helpful in explaining how the responses to the Request came about. He said in his statement:- "8...I can confirm that this response was issued by one of my colleagues on the FOI team. The staff member had referred the Appellant's request to the DVLA Policy team who in turn advised that no information about the requirement to return expired driving licences ("the Surrender Requirement") should be released to the Appellant with reference to section 35 of FOIA. However, they did not inform my colleague whether any specific information was held and nor did my colleague enquire further as to what information was actually held. Instead, my colleague took this response at face value and issued the response to the Appellant's request to confirm that information was held but was exempt. This was the wrong response because the request was not for information generally about the Surrender Requirement; it was for "pre-specified terms of reference" for the review of the Surrender Requirement"

67. He said at the hearing that the Request went to the DVLA's driving licence policy team because, based on the interpretation of the Request, that team was the most likely to hold any in-scope information. He said that what should have happened is that when the response was receive from the policy team the FOIA team should have gone back to check what was actually held and obtain copies of anything and the policy team should have provided anything for the FOIA to check it.

68. The required process was not followed and the evidence given gave the impression that the FOIA team at DVLA simply forwarded on the Request to the policy team without guidance about what they should look for, how they should look for it, the depth of that exercise, the timescale and how to ensure this methodology was recorded. No reference was made for example to the Guidance. We also gained the impression that when the policy team responded it told the FOIA team what was to be done and also told them that the exemption at section 35 was to be applied. We accept that organizations may structure themselves in such a way and make such a process work well. However not in this case because for example only:- (a) Mr Chatham told us that the required process had not been followed. (b) the policy team did not pick up on the fact that the document for which they required section 35 to be applied was not in-scope and made no reference to their view on the competing arguments on the PIBT. (c) the people who dealt with it in the FOIA team at that time appear to have lacked the ability, will or curiosity to challenge this response or provide expert oversight on what the policy team was saying- not even when an internal review was requested. Summary

69. In summary:- (a) the Draft Submission provided in the CB was not itself held when the Request was received. (b) the Pro-Forma is a ToR and in-scope and so is to be provided to the Appellant unless DVLA asserts (other than it is not a ToR) why it is to be withheld. (c) we do not accept that, on the balance of probabilities, DVLA held no in-scope information, at the date the Request was received, other than the Pro-Forma. Decision

70. For the reasons set out above the DN was not in accordance with the law and the appeal is allowed. Signed Judge Heald Date: 2 March 2026
